theory.overview: Dynamic arrays are a fundamental data structure that automatically resize themselves when they reach capacity. Unlike static arrays with fixed size, dynamic arrays grow (typically doubling in size) to accommodate new elements while maintaining amortized O(1) insertion time. This makes them the backbone of modern programming - Python lists, Java ArrayLists, and C++ vectors are all dynamic array implementations.

keyConcepts.name: Amortized O(1) Time
keyConcepts.description: While individual resize operations are O(n), the doubling strategy ensures that over many operations, the average cost per insertion remains constant. This is because resizing becomes exponentially less frequent as the array grows.

keyConcepts.name: Growth Factor
keyConcepts.description: Most implementations use a growth factor of 1.5x or 2x. A 2x factor provides simpler amortized analysis, while 1.5x is more memory-efficient. The choice affects the trade-off between memory usage and copy operations.

keyConcepts.name: Capacity vs Size
keyConcepts.description: Size refers to the actual number of elements stored, while capacity is the total space available. The array only resizes when size equals capacity, leaving headroom for future insertions.

keyConcepts.name: Geometric Expansion
keyConcepts.description: By growing geometrically (multiplying by a constant factor) rather than arithmetically (adding a constant amount), we ensure that the cost of copying elements during resize is spread across many cheap insertions.

algorithmSteps.description: Push 5 - size < capacity, insert at index 0

minigame.title: Perfect Timing
minigame.description: Resize the array exactly when it reaches capacity. Too early wastes memory, too late loses data.
instructions: Push elements until the array is full
